background.title: Atoms, ions and reading a formula
background.html:
Everything is made of tiny atoms. An element has only one kind of atom (C, O, Na). A compound has two or more elements joined. Some compounds are molecules (small groups of atoms, such as CO2); others are made of ions, atoms with a charge such as Na+ and Cl−.

A formula counts atoms. The small low number counts the atom just before it; a bracket multiplies everything inside.

FormulaAtoms in one unit
CO21 C, 2 O
Ca(NO3)21 Ca, 2 N, 6 O
MgCl2ions: 1 Mg2+ and 2 Cl−

background.title: Reading and balancing a chemical equation
background.html:
An equation shows a reaction: reactants (what you start with) on the left, products (what is made) on the right, and the arrow means "react to make".

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)

Atoms are never created or destroyed, so each kind of atom must have the same count on both sides. Here: Mg 1 = 1, H 2 = 2, Cl 2 = 2. To balance, you change only the big numbers in front (the coefficients). 2H2O means two molecules, so 4 H and 2 O. Changing a small number would make a different substance.

The letters in brackets show the physical form: (s) solid (this includes a precipitate, a solid that forms in a solution), (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.

background.title: Standard form and significant figures
background.html:
Huge and tiny numbers are written as a number of at least 1 but less than 10, times a power of ten: 6.02 × 1023 is 602 followed by 21 zeros. A negative power means a small number: 10−3 = 0.001.

On the calculator use the ×10x (or EXP) key, not "× 10 ^" typed by hand, so 6.02 × 1023 stays one number. Check: 0.0500 × 6.02 × 1023 = 3.01 × 1022. If you get 12.04 × 1022, rewrite it as 1.204 × 1023.

Significant figures are the digits that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit. 0.0500 has 3 (5, 0, 0). Give answers to the same number as the data, usually 3: 19.83 becomes 19.8.

background.title: Ratios and proportion
background.html:
A ratio a : b compares two amounts. In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O the ratio H2 : O2 is 2 : 1, so 0.30 mol of O2 needs 2 × 0.30 = 0.60 mol of H2. To go from what you know to what you want, multiply by (number wanted ÷ number known).

Directly proportional: double one, the other doubles (V and T in kelvin). The graph is a straight line through (0, 0).

Inversely proportional: double one, the other halves, so multiplying them always gives the same number. For a gas, 100 kPa × 2.0 dm3 = 200, so at 200 kPa the volume is 200 ÷ 200 = 1.0 dm3.

background.title: Rearranging a formula and substituting
background.html:
A formula links letters. To find a different letter, get it on its own by doing the same thing to both sides.

  • n = m ÷ M. Multiply both sides by M: m = n × M. Then divide by n: M = m ÷ n.
  • PV = nRT. Divide both sides by P: V = nRT ÷ P.

Then substitute: put the numbers in place of the letters, in the right units. Example: n = 0.200 mol, R = 8.31, T = 300 K, P = 150 000 Pa gives V = 0.200 × 8.31 × 300 ÷ 150 000 = 3.32 × 10−3 m3.

Rearrange first, substitute second: it is easier to check and earns the method marks.

background.title: Letters, units and converting them
background.html:
LetterMeansUnit
namount (moles)mol
mmassg
Mmolar massg mol−1
C or [X]concentrationmol dm−3
V, P, Tvolume, pressure, temperaturedm3 or m3, Pa, K

A power of −1 on a unit means "per": g mol−1 is grams per mole. n(Mg) means "amount of Mg". A small 1 or 2 after a letter means before and after a change: P1 is the starting pressure, P2 the new one.

  • Volume: 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3; 1 m3 = 1000 dm3. So 250 cm3 = 0.250 dm3 = 2.50 × 10−4 m3.
  • Pressure: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa, so 101 kPa = 1.01 × 105 Pa.
  • Temperature: K = °C + 273.15, so 25 °C = 298 K.

background.title: What gas pressure and temperature mean
background.html:
A gas is made of particles far apart, moving fast in all directions. Each time a particle hits the container wall it gives a tiny push. All those pushes on each square metre of wall are the pressure. More hits, or harder hits, mean higher pressure.

Temperature measures how fast the particles move (their energy of movement). Hotter means faster, so they hit the walls more often and harder. In a rigid container the volume cannot change, so heating the gas raises its pressure.

The kelvin scale starts at the coldest possible point, 0 K, so a kelvin temperature is in proportion to that energy. That is why gas calculations need kelvin. Heating from 20 °C to 40 °C does not double anything: it is 293 K to 313 K, only about 7% hotter.

background.title: Command words: how much to write
background.html:
Each IB question, and each "I can" line, starts with a command word. It tells you how much to write, so read it first. Every command word on this page is underlined: tap it for its meaning.

What to writeCommand words
a name, a value or a short answer, no reasonsState, Identify
a number, with the steps of your workingCalculate, Determine, Solve
a graph showing the shape, with labelled axesSketch
reasons, a conclusion or a possible answerExplain, Deduce, Distinguish, Suggest
several points and a conclusionAnalyse, Discuss

The more a command word asks for, the more marks the question usually carries.

terms.def: The smallest particle of an element. A water molecule, for example, is 2 hydrogen atoms joined to 1 oxygen atom.
A substance made of only one kind of atom, such as carbon (C) or oxygen (O). Each element has its own symbol and its own place in the periodic table (the chart of all the elements).
A substance made of two or more elements joined together in a fixed ratio, such as water (H<sub>2</sub>O) or salt (NaCl).
A small group of atoms joined together. H<sub>2</sub>O is one molecule: 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge, because it has lost or gained electrons. Na<sup>+</sup> has lost one electron; Cl<sup>−</sup> has gained one.
A tiny particle with a negative charge. Electrons move around the centre (nucleus) of every atom.
One particular kind of chemical, such as water, oxygen or sodium chloride.
A general word for the tiny pieces that matter is made of: atoms, molecules or ions. In an answer, use the exact word the question needs.
A small number written low after a symbol. In H<sub>2</sub>O the 2 is a subscript: 2 hydrogen atoms. Changing it changes the substance.
Made of ions. An ionic compound such as NaCl is a huge regular pattern of positive and negative ions, so it has no separate molecules.
A structure where enormous numbers of atoms or ions are joined in one continuous network, like diamond or salt. There is no small molecule to count.
The group of ions shown by the formula of an ionic compound. One formula unit of NaCl is one Na<sup>+</sup> and one Cl<sup>−</sup>.
An equation that shows only the ions that actually change in a reaction, leaving out the ions that stay the same in the solution.
A substance you start with in a reaction; it gets used up. It is written on the left of the arrow.
A new substance made in a reaction. It is written on the right of the arrow.
A chemical equation with the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. The big numbers in front give the mole ratio.
The big number in front of a formula in an equation. In 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O the coefficients are 2, 1 and 2: they give the mole ratio, 2 : 1 : 2.
Letters in brackets after each formula: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.
The number relationships in a reaction: how many moles of each substance react and form, read from the balanced equation.
Burning: a reaction with oxygen that gives out heat. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives only CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O.
A compound made of only carbon and hydrogen atoms, such as methane CH<sub>4</sub> or propane C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>.
HCl dissolved in water. It reacts with metals such as magnesium and zinc to give hydrogen gas and a salt (a compound such as MgCl<sub>2</sub>).
The chemist's counting unit, symbol mol. One mole is 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> particles, the way one dozen is 12. Chemists count particles in moles because they are far too many to count one by one.
How many moles of one substance go with how many moles of another, read from the coefficients. In 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub> : O<sub>2</sub> = 2 : 1.
The chemist's name for "how many particles", measured in moles (symbol n). It is not the same as mass.
The number of particles in one mole: N<sub>A</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> (per mole).
Equal volumes of any gases, at the same temperature and pressure, hold the same number of molecules. So for gases, the volume ratio equals the mole ratio.
How heavy an element's average atom is compared with a carbon-12 atom (which counts as exactly 12). Symbol A<sub>r</sub>, no units. Carbon is 12.01.
The A<sub>r</sub> values of every atom in the formula added up. Symbol M<sub>r</sub>, no units. H<sub>2</sub>O: 2 × 1.01 + 16.00 = 18.02.
An average where the more common values count more. About three quarters of chlorine atoms have mass 35 and one quarter 37, so the average (35.45) is closer to 35.
The most common kind of carbon atom. It is the standard for atomic masses: one carbon-12 atom has a relative mass of exactly 12, and every other atom is compared with it.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams, unit g mol<sup>−1</sup>. It has the same number as M<sub>r</sub>: water is 18.02 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. Glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O (everything divided by 6).
The actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule, such as C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> for glucose. It is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
What something is made of, and how much of each part. Percentage composition by mass: the percentage of the total mass that each element makes up.
How much of a substance is dissolved in each dm<sup>3</sup> of solution: in mol dm<sup>−3</sup> (moles per dm<sup>3</sup>) or g dm<sup>−3</sup> (grams per dm<sup>3</sup>).
The liquid you get when a substance dissolves evenly in another, such as salt in water. The whole mixture is the solution.
The substance that dissolves, such as the salt in salt water.
The liquid that does the dissolving, usually water.
Adding more water to a solution. The moles of solute stay the same but are spread through a bigger volume, so the concentration goes down.
Water is added until the total volume of the solution is exactly that value, usually in a flask marked with that volume. It is the final volume, not the volume of water added.
A lab method to find a concentration: one solution is added slowly from a tube with a volume scale (a burette) to a measured volume of another, until the reaction is just complete.
A titration in two steps: add a known excess of one reactant, then titrate what is left over to work out how much actually reacted.
Water molecules that are part of a crystal and its formula, such as the 5H<sub>2</sub>O in blue copper sulfate, CuSO<sub>4</sub>·5H<sub>2</sub>O.
A solid that forms in a liquid during a reaction and does not dissolve, so it can be filtered off.
More than is needed. A reactant in excess is not all used up: some is left over at the end.
The reactant that runs out first. It stops the reaction, so it decides how much product can form.
The amount of product. Theoretical yield: the most you could get, calculated from the equation. Experimental yield: what you actually get. Percentage yield compares the two.
The percentage of the total mass of the reactants that ends up in the product you want. 100% means no atoms are wasted.
Other reactions happening at the same time as the one you want. They use up reactants to make unwanted products.
A reversible reaction can also go backwards (products turning back into reactants), so it never fully finishes.
Unwanted other substances mixed into your product. They add to its mass.
Removing impurities to leave the pure product, for example by washing it and filtering it (pouring through filter paper so the solid stays behind).
Yeast turning sugar (glucose) into ethanol (the alcohol in drinks) and carbon dioxide, as in making bread or wine.
A reaction that adds water to a molecule. Hydration of ethene: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH.
Designing chemical processes that waste less, use less energy and avoid harmful substances.
An imagined, perfect gas that follows PV = nRT exactly. Real gases come close at high temperature and low pressure.
An actual gas, such as nitrogen or CO<sub>2</sub>. Its particles do take up some space and do attract each other a little, so it is not quite ideal.
A simplified picture used to explain and predict how something behaves. It leaves out some details on purpose.
Something taken as true to keep a model simple, even if it is not exactly true.
Moving in straight lines in all directions and at many speeds, with no pattern, changing direction at each collision.
So small that it can be ignored.
Weak attractions between separate molecules (not the strong links that hold the atoms of one molecule together). They pull gas particles towards each other a little.
An elastic collision is a perfect bounce: the particles lose no kinetic energy overall, like ideal snooker balls.
The energy something has because it is moving. Faster particles have more kinetic energy; a higher temperature means faster particles.
To move away from what is expected. A real gas deviates from ideal behaviour when PV = nRT no longer gives quite the right answer.

A polar molecule has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end (water is one), so polar molecules attract each other more. Non-polar particles, such as helium atoms or methane molecules, do not.
To turn from a gas into a liquid when cooled, like steam on a cold window.
The push of a gas on each square metre of the container wall, caused by particles hitting it. Unit: pascal (Pa).
Pa (pascal) is the SI unit of pressure, and 1 kPa (kilopascal) = 1000 Pa. Air pressure is about 100 kPa = 100 000 Pa. Change kPa to Pa before using PV = nRT.
The SI temperature scale, symbol K. It starts at the coldest possible temperature (0 K = −273.15 °C), so K = °C + 273.15. Gas calculations always need kelvin.
Standard temperature and pressure: 273.15 K (0 °C) and 100 kPa. At STP one mole of any ideal gas takes up 22.7 dm<sup>3</sup>.
The volume taken up by one mole of a gas. It is the same for every ideal gas at the same temperature and pressure: 22.7 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> at STP.
R = 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>, a fixed number used in PV = nRT.
The international standard units of science, such as metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and mole. Pascal (Pa) and cubic metre (m<sup>3</sup>) are built from them.
The same amount of gas the whole time: none is added and none escapes, so n does not change.
Not changing. "At constant T" means the temperature is kept the same. "Constant motion" means moving all the time without stopping.

Inversely proportional: when one quantity doubles, the other halves, so multiplying them gives the same number each time (P × V). An inverse relationship (inversely related) is looser: when one goes up, the other goes down.
The point (0, 0) on a graph, where the two axes cross.
Extended beyond the measured points by continuing the line in the same way.
Stiff, so it cannot change shape. A rigid can keeps the same volume.
Moles per cubic decimetre, the unit of concentration. 0.10 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> means 0.10 mol in every 1 dm<sup>3</sup> of solution.
Grams per cubic decimetre: concentration by mass. Change mol dm<sup>−3</sup> to g dm<sup>−3</sup> by multiplying by M.
Grams per mole, the unit of molar mass. A power of −1 on a unit means "per".
Joules per kelvin per mole, the unit of R. The joule (J) is the unit of energy.
Cubic decimetre, a volume: a cube 10 cm on each side. 1 dm<sup>3</sup> = 1 litre = 1000 cm<sup>3</sup> = 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.
Cubic centimetre, a small volume: 1 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1 mL. 1000 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1 dm<sup>3</sup>, and 10<sup>6</sup> cm<sup>3</sup> = 1 m<sup>3</sup>.
Here: one of the numbered learning points in the official IB guide (such as 1.4.5). Each one can be examined.
A booklet of formulas, constants and data (such as the A<sub>r</sub> values) that you get in every IB Chemistry exam. You must know what is in it and how to use it.
The IB Chemistry guide lists "Tools": skills used in practical work. Tool 1 is experimental techniques, such as measuring masses and volumes accurately.
IB command term: give a specific name, value or other brief answer, without explanation or calculation.
To work out a number. As an IB command term: obtain a numerical answer, showing the important steps of your working.
IB command term: reach a conclusion from the information given.
Pick out the right answer from the possibilities, for example which reactant is limiting. IB questions use it, though it is not on the 2025 chemistry list of command terms.
To give reasons or causes. As an IB command term: give a detailed account including reasons or causes.
IB command term: propose a possible answer or solution.
IB command term "sketch": draw a diagram or graph showing the general shape or relationship and the important features, labelled. It does not need exact values.
IB command term: obtain the only possible answer. Usually this means working it out by calculation, such as finding M<sub>r</sub> from the A<sub>r</sub> values.
Work out the answer to a problem, usually by putting the given numbers into a formula. Show the steps of your working, as for "calculate".
Convert both ways. Here: from percentage composition to the empirical formula, and from a formula back to the percentages.
Change a value into another form or unit without changing what it means: 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.250 dm<sup>3</sup>, or 0.500 mol of atoms = 3.01 × 10<sup>23</sup> atoms.
Show clearly how two things are different. Here: the yield you calculate from the equation (theoretical) and the yield you actually get (experimental).
Look closely and pick out the key features. For a graph: its shape, whether the line goes through the origin, and what that tells you about the two quantities.
IB command term: give a balanced review with several points or arguments, and a clear conclusion backed up by evidence. It needs a longer answer than "explain".
Find out by doing experiments or studying results, for example measuring how the volume of a gas changes as you heat it.
A quantity that can change, such as pressure, volume or temperature. A graph shows how one variable changes when another one does.
One of the two lines along the edges of a graph, each with a scale. "P against V" means P on the up-and-down axis and V on the left-to-right axis.
A weak point: a case where something stops working well. A limitation of the ideal gas model is that real gases do not follow it exactly.
Named exactly. "Specified entities" means you must say what you are counting: atoms, molecules, ions or something else.
The single thing you are counting in moles: one atom, one molecule, one ion, one electron or one formula unit.
To measure something or give it as a number.
The size of single atoms and molecules: far too small to see, and far too many to count one by one.
To break down into simpler substances. In 2NaN<sub>3</sub> → 2Na + 3N<sub>2</sub> one compound breaks into two elements.
Squeezed into a smaller volume.
To take up space. "What volume does the gas occupy?" means "how much space does it fill?"
In the form of a gas.
Pouring a mixture through filter paper: the liquid runs through and the solid stays behind on the paper.
The digits after the decimal point. 12.01 is written to two decimal places.
The digits that carry meaning, counted from the first digit that is not zero. 0.0500 has 3 significant figures. Give answers to the same number as the data, usually 3.
The coldest possible temperature: 0 K, which is −273.15 °C. Nothing can be colder.

P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub> for a fixed mass of gas: 1 means before a change, 2 means after. Use it when pressure, volume and temperature change together.
A skeleton equation has the right formulas but is not balanced yet: the big numbers in front are still missing.
The amount wasted: material that ends up in products nobody wants.
How well something turns what goes in into what you want out. Here: how much of the reactants' mass ends up in the wanted product.
The product you want to make. In atom economy every other product counts as waste.
When particles hit each other or hit the container wall. To collide means to hit.
C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, the alcohol in drinks. It is also used as a fuel.
A hydrocarbon gas, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, made from crude oil. It easily adds on other small molecules, such as water.
A sugar, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>. Plants make it, and your body uses it for energy.
